**Introduction**

As an attorney, I spend a large amount of my time assisting clients in obtaining relief from conflict and confusion. The greatest satis faction in my work is providing my clients counsel that allows them to *prevent* facing any such obstacles. As a legal self-help author, I am hopefully able to help provide this guidance on a much larger scale and in much greater detail. When asked by this book’s publisher to write a book that would assist those seeking to sell their own homes, I was intrigued by the prospect of helping people with a process that is so commonly encountered, so impor tant, and yet so misunderstood. 

The topic of the book coincided with a new trend I have been witnessing. In my real estate practice, I have never seen so much interest on the part of homeowners looking to sell their homes themselves as I have in this past year or so. After doing some research, I was able to see that my personal observations of my local area are quite consistent with the national trend.  

One reason why the United States is the greatest country in the world is because of the great choices we have. Americans always insist on having choices in their lives. Individuals and   
xii Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

companies prosper when they are able to provide alternative products, services, and methods that satisfy this need. This demand for more options has recently spilled over into the home sales sector. As a result of new technology, ideas, and methods, homeowners now have the choice between using a conventional real estate agent and selling their own home by themselves.  

In the first chapter of this book, some possible reasons for the advent of the *for-sale-by-owner* phenomenon are considered, as well as why more and more homeowners are choosing this option. The various types of homeowners who can expect to have the best chance of success selling their own homes are also explored. 

Chapter 2 examines the need to consider, at the outset, your options for future housing prior to setting out with selling your home. The pitfalls associated with buying another house before selling yours are discussed, and the options available when the home seller needs to find a new place to live prior to the sale date are evaluated.  

Whereas Chapter 2 focuses on preparing yourself for the pending move and its implications, Chapter 3 begins by focusing on preparing your home to make it *ready for the public*. This chapter looks into the best and most cost-effective ways to make improve ments to the home, and reveals tips on how to make the home look newer, larger, and cleaner. In the last sections of Chapter 3, the importance of retaining an attorney at this early stage so that he or she can be there for you throughout the entire process is discussed. The value of a real estate attorney is examined, and specific rec ommendations for choosing and retaining a capable one are made. 

Chapter 4 begins the journey into the important area of mar keting your home. Assigning the right price is the most critical aspect of your marketing plan. The formal and informal approaches to determining your home’s value are analyzed in detail. Next, the seller is able to provide prospective buyers with all of the home’s critical information at a glance by compiling a *listing sheet*. The elements that comprise the listing sheet are  
Introduction xiii 

carefully reviewed, and suggestions on how to prepare the sheet to make your home stand out are given. A sample listing sheet is included for illustrative purposes. 

Chapter 5 is dedicated to the vital element of advertising. Professional real estate agencies often write very effective ads that entice buyers and make them want to find out more. These agencies help *by-owner* sellers by helping them refine what is said in their ad and how to say it. The federal *Fair Housing Act* is reviewed and its effect on homes-for-sale advertising is discussed. The chapter concludes with a detailed analysis of the most effec tive places to advertise and how to best utilize each.  

A prospective buyer can be lured with smart advertising, but the sale is made or lost after the home’s viewing. Chapter 6 focuses on the art of showing your home to the prospective buyer, whether it be through an open house or a one-on-one tour. Where and how to advertise the open house and the very important steps the home owner should take prior to the *showing* are reviewed. The goal to showing your house is to help make a buyer fall in love with your home just as you did when you first saw it. The documents and items that you need to have on hand and give to your buyer to make the viewing process complete and professional are set out. Reviewed are some well-tested methods of how to conduct the actual home tour, what to say, and how to comply with disclosure laws. 

Once an interested buyer comes forth and offers to buy your home, you need to negotiate the terms of the sale. Contracts for the sale of real estate must be in writing. Chapter 7 advises where these written contracts (*Purchase and Sale Agreements*) can be obtained and what components they must include. Some time-tested advice, as well as actual language that can be inserted in the agreement for your pro tection (and advantage) are provided. Further, some tips on how to best respond to some of the common provisions that buyers seek to insert in the agreements are examined. The chapter concludes with specifics on how to effectively execute the agreement.  
xiv Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

Chapter 8 spotlights some scenarios that a seller may encounter after a buyer steps forward. It offers answers to questions about how best to handle buyers and prepare for the closing. This chapter will help make you an informed seller, so you will know how to approach and deftly handle these matters. 

Chapter 9 examines the home-selling process at the closing. The various documents that a seller will need to have for the closing are itemized and described. Next discussed are the two dif ferent types of closings: the attorney/conference table closing and the title company/escrow closing. To provide you with a better understanding of what you can expect to sign at the closing, each of the common documents are reviewed and their purposes revealed. Copies of a few of the actual documents are provided for illustrative purposes. 

For those who occupy the homes they are selling, Chapter 10 probes the world of moving and storage. Tips provided by experts on how to make the moving experience less stressful and less costly are included. Also investigated are the insurance options provided by moving companies to determine the right one for you. 

Chapter 11 concludes the book with a special look at how to handle the *hard-to-sell* home. The reasons why some homes may be difficult to sell are examined and advice is offered for selling each specific type of hard-to-sell home. If the reason your home does not sell in a timely fashion is not explained by one of the hard-to-sell categories, some additional solutions are presented. For those who want to revert back to the traditional selling process of using a real estate broker, a detailed plan for hiring a first-rate, full-commission broker is included.  

It was my honor to be asked to write this book, and it was my pleasure to write it for you. I hope that it serves as a useful tool as you engage upon the adventurous journey of selling your own home.  

Best Wishes, 

Joseph P. DiBlasi  
CHAPTER 1 

**Frequently Asked**   
**Why Sell by Owner? Questions**

**1\. What is the Multiple Listing Service (MLS)?** The *Multiple Listing Service*, frequently identified by its initials—MLS, is a service by the National Association of Realtors and its affiliate, the *National Association of Real Estate Boards*. MLS was created at the turn of the twentieth century to allow for an exchange of information among real estate brokers for their home listings. There is a Multiple Listing Service for each of the geographical National Association of Real Estate Board members throughout the country. At its core, the MLS is a database of property-listing information that is made avail able exclusively to member brokers and agents to assist them in the marketing of their customers’ homes. The MLS is controlled by rules and regulations. One such rule requires that a listing broker disclose the compensation to be paid to a broker who procures the eventual buyer for a particular home. 

**2\. Isn’t there too much for me to know in order to sell my own home?** 

No. Despite what the real estate broker industry may want you to think, you are perfectly able to sell your own home. In fact, who   
xvi Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

else knows more about your home and its neighborhood than you? With the help of this book, a good for-sale-by-owner Internet site, and a trusted real estate attorney, you will have access to all of the skills, tools, and information needed to do a fine job of selling your home and save yourself thousands of dollars in the process. 

**3\. What are the most costly mistakes that a for-sale-by owner (FSBO) seller makes?** 

Unfortunately, many FSBO sellers are too quick to market their own homes to save the broker’s commission without undergoing some necessary planning. Many fail to accurately and objectively determine the fair market value of their home, and as a result, set an asking price that is too high. Others use lawn signs and other marketing tools that look very amateurish and give off an impres sion to potential buyers that the purchase process may be fraught with problems. Other sellers who do locate an interested party do not have the proper contracts ready and consequently try to put a deal together using a homemade contract that will leave them vul nerable to problems. FSBO sellers have the potential for saving many thousands of dollars, but some planning is necessary. 

**4\. Am I better off using a broker when it is a buyer’s market?** 

Not necessarily. A *buyer’s market* indicates one or more of the fol lowing: the economy is slow, interest rates are high, or there are more homes for sale than there are buyers. A buyer’s market requires a home seller to be extra competitive. As a FSBO seller, you have a distinct advantage over those home sellers using brokers, in that you can be much more flexible in the selling price of your home—you are not paying a 5% or 6% commission. If you use the marketing methods detailed in this book and price your home smartly, buyers will notice your home’s great value.   
Frequently Asked Questions xvii 

**5\. I found a buyer and he has an attorney who will write up all the necessary documents and contracts for the sale. Can I proceed through closing without hiring my own attorney since the buyer’s attorney will take care of everything?** 

You would be making a very significant and potentially costly error. Remember, the buyer’s attorney owes a duty to zealously represent and advocate for his or her client—the buyer. The buyer’s attorney owes you nothing. Consequently, the buyer’s attorney may insert provisions in the purchase agreements that are favorable to and pro tective of the buyer, but that are not good for you. In addition, it is common for obstacles to arise after the agreement is signed. Title defects, the buyer’s financing problems, the buyer’s requests to move in before closing, and unknown charges appearing on the settlement statement are just a few examples of when you will greatly benefit to have your own attorney by your side. As the buyer has his or her loan officer, attorney, bank attorney, and possibly even a buyer’s broker available to assist him or her through the process, you should counter this with your own counsel. Moreover, when you examine how much money is at stake in the transaction (the selling price of the home) and how much you are saving by not using a broker, the typ ical, flat-rate fee charged by most real estate attorneys to handle a seller’s closing is a sound investment. 

**6\. I was so excited to receive an offer by a prospective buyer for full asking price. However, after signing my acceptance, I now doubt that I will find a suitable new home in time to sell on the date for closing stated in the buyer’s offer. Can I change the date? Or when we sign the second of the two agreements, can I make the sale contingent on our finding a new home?** 

A party may not make unilateral changes to an executed agree ment. Any changes to terms that have already been agreed upon (such as a price, closing date, and the terms of any contingencies)  
xviii Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

can only be changed if both parties agree. Therefore, you will not be able to change the date of the closing unless your buyer agrees. If he or she does not agree and you refuse to close on the agreed upon date, he or she likely will be able to have a court enforce the agreement and force you to sell and move on the stipulated date. If you live in an area that traditionally uses two agreements in the purchase process (i.e., an *Offer to Purchase* and a *Purchase and Sale Agreement*), the terms of the first agreement are biding and cannot be changed in the second agreement, unless both sides agree to the change. In this situation, you will not be able to insert “contingent upon seller finding suitable housing” language without the buyer’s agreement, as it was not part of the accepted offer. 

**7\. When I bought the home that I am now selling, I purchased an owner’s title insurance policy as well as a lender’s title insurance policy. What exactly is title insurance and how will this benefit me now that I am selling?** 

Title insurance is a form of insurance, like health, life, or auto mobile. Instead of insuring against medical bills, death, or dam age to your vehicle, it insures you against defects that affect the quality of your title to your home, the single largest asset for most people. There are two types of title insurance—owner’s and lender’s. When you buy a home with the help of a mortgage loan, the lender will require that, as part of your closing costs, you pay for a policy that protects the lender from anything that could jeopardize it from being the first lien on your property. You also have the option of buying a separate policy for yourself as the owner. An owner’s policy will guarantee that your full rights to ownership are protected and not compromised by any claim or defect, from the beginning of time until the date of the policy. Unlike the other types of insurance policies, title insurance has a one-time premium, not an annual one. It insures you for the life of your ownership of the home.  
Frequently Asked Questions xix 

If you did not need the policy during your ownership, that is good news. However, often times a title issue does not make itself known until you try to sell the home. When a buyer prepares to buy your home, a title examination is performed. (Some states cus toms require the seller to pay and undertake the title examination, while in others the buyer is responsible.) The title examination will reveal any problems that need to be remedied before you can pass a good title to the buyer. If the title examination reveals prob lems that were caused during your ownership and after you pur chased title insurance, such as someone suing you and obtaining an attachment, the policy will likely not provide protection and you will need to rectify the problem yourself. However, if the problem arose before the date of your policy, you will be able to have the title insurance company assist you in curing the defect so that you can sell your property as scheduled. Examples of where your policy may protect you upon selling your home include:  

• mortgages that show up as outstanding and not discharged;  • an easement that allows for the construction of a road;  • deeds or wills that contain improper wording or names;  • an unknown heir of a prior owner who now claims ownership; and,  

• improperly recorded documents.  

**8\. I listed my home as for sale by owner and now am I receiving many calls from local brokers who want me to list with them. They tell me that they have buyers already identified for my home. What should I do?** 

The only individuals who are searching those for-sale-by-owner newspaper and online listings more ambitiously than prospective buyers are real estate brokers. As a FSBO seller, you, by defini tion, have identified yourself as both eager to sell your home and not contractually bound to any broker—the perfect target for a broker looking to increase his or her listings. Unfortunately, some brokers, as part of their selling pitch to have you sign a listing  
xx Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

agreement, will deceptively tell you that they have buyers waiting in the wings to buy a home *just like yours*. (As you will see later in this book, most brokers utilize exclusive right to sell listing agreements, which means they will be entitled to a listing com mission regardless of who ultimately finds the buyer. While that *buyer* they had *waiting in the wings* unfortunately found another house, you will be contractually obligated to pay the broker as long as your house sells during your contract period—which can be six months or more.)  

Your response to these broker calls may vary depending on the market condition and your specific situation. If you are in a seller’s market with low interest rates, a shortage of homes for sale, a good local economy, or an abundance of buyers, and have just begun marketing the house with every expectation that it will sell quickly, you may want to politely advise the broker that you will continue marketing it yourself. However, if the market is somewhat less than perfect for sellers or you already have spent considerable time and effort in marketing it yourself without suc cess, you may want to inform them that you are not willing to hire them to list your home, but that you would certainly enter tain paying them a commission upon their procuring their buyer. Finally, if you have been trying to sell your home yourself, and despite reading this book and using all of the tools and tech niques at your disposal, you are at your wits end, you may want to give the listing to one of the brokers who has called you and made a good impression. Before you do, refer to Chapter 11 of this book to help you select the best possible full-service broker. 

**9\. Who are the various players that I can expect to hear about or come in contact with during my home sale process, and what are their respective roles?** 

Here is a brief description of the players in the approximate order that you may expect to hear about or encounter them.  
Frequently Asked Questions xxi 

*Your (seller’s) attorney.* Responsible for representing and coun seling you (and only you) through the entire process (or that por tion of the process for which you retain him or her). Ideally, as a FSBO seller, you should consult and retain an attorney at the very earliest point, such as when you first decide to sell your home your self. He or she will likely be your only advisor and will be valuable to you. The role and duties of the seller’s attorney are more specif ically detailed in Chapter 3\. 

*Real estate broker.* A real estate broker is licensed by the state to market and sell real estate. A broker may have various salespeople working under him or her in the office. A listing broker is the broker who is retained under contract by the seller to list his or her home for sale. With an FSBO seller, there is no listing broker. A selling broker is the broker who finds and procures the eventual buyer for a home seller. When an FSBO seller engages the services of a flat-fee broker, a broker sponsors the FSBO seller so that he or she may be listed in the multiple listing service, and the FSBO seller will need to agree to a set compensation for the selling broker. A broker who finds a buyer for an FSBO seller typically is a buyer’s broker, meaning that he or she is working on behalf of the buyer and has no obligation to the seller. 

*Prospective buyer.* The prospective buyer has the duty of pur chasing your home in accordance with the terms of the executed purchase agreement. 

*Buyer’s attorney.* The buyer’s attorney is retained by the buyer to protect his or her interests in the purchase of the home. The attor ney will negotiate the terms of the deal, draft up provisions to include in any documents, counsel the buyer throughout the entire process, and advocate for the buyer to make sure the terms of the written agreement are upheld by the seller. He or she will also attend the closing to explain all of the documents and numbers to the buyer, and ensure the buyer’s interests are protected. 

*Lender.* This is the bank or lending institution obtained by your buyer to loan him or her the funds necessary to purchase your  
xxii Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

home. When a lender issues a commitment to the buyer, it is con tractually obligated to loan him or her the money, subject to any express conditions only. A lender may take the form of a small community bank, a large national bank, a credit union, a mortgage broker (a middle-man type of firm that searches for a satisfactory, licensed lender to make the deal work), or a mortgage lender. In addition, a private individual may also act as a lender. 

*Loan officer.* This is usually the point person of the lender who serves as the buyer’s primary contact. A loan officer has the pri mary duty of assisting the buyer with the completion of the mort gage application and finding the right loan program for the buyer’s needs. Typically, the buyer may provide you with the loan officer’s name, but other than that, the loan officer has little (if any) direct contact with the seller.  

*Home inspector.* This person is retained by the buyer pursuant to the purchase agreement’s home inspection contingency. He or she is likely a current or former tradesperson or building inspector, and will conduct a thorough inspection of your home and all of its com ponents and systems. The home inspector usually drafts up a lengthy written report as a by-product of the home inspection.  

*Appraiser.* This individual is retained by the buyer’s lender to go to your home, investigate all of its qualities and particulars, and compare it to other recent sales in the area to determine the home’s fair market value. An appraiser is licensed by the state, and receives significant education and training to know how to value real estate. The appraiser drafts up a report that shows the home and how it compares to other similar properties, and then establishes the property’s fair market value. The lender will use the appraisal to determine how much money it will agree to lend to the buyer.  

*Loan underwriter/loan committee.* This person or group of people works for the lender and is responsible for making sure the buyer is qualified to obtain the loan applied for. They will set limits to the amount of the loan, and will specify what information is required  
Frequently Asked Questions xxiii 

about the buyer and your home so the loan may be approved. You will likely not have occasion to deal directly with the underwriter or the loan committee. 

*Title examiner/abstractor.* This person is hired by the settlement agent to perform a search of your title at the applicable county recorder’s office or registry of deeds. He or she will perform a tech nical search process, whereby the documents constituting the chain of title are examined and traced from you, back to your seller, and the seller before, and so on, until the requisite number of years is covered to satisfy state legal procedures. Once the title examiner goes back the requisite number of years, he or she will trace the documents back to the present. The title examiner then writes up a summary report of what was found and forwards it to the settle ment agent, who will examine the report. If a title defect is found, he or she will apprise the seller or his or her attorney, so it may be remedied prior to closing, if possible. 

*Settlement agent.* This is the generic title given to the person or firm who acts to undertake a title examination of the property and coordinates the transfer of the deed, all monies, and other documents to effectuate the transfer of title from the seller to the buyer. Your pro ceeds check will come from the settlement agent. Depending on your geographic location, the settlement agent’s duties may be performed by the *bank attorney* or a *title company*. 

**10\. My home is older and in need of significant reha bilitation. I want to sell but do not have the cash on hand to make the repairs needed to get it in top condition. Any suggestions?** 

After obtaining an appraisal to determine the fair market value of your home, you may want to speak with a few local contractors or builders to see if they would be interested in purchasing the home. Your attorney would be a good resource to use to seek out these potential buyers, as he or she likely knows the local builders and contractors in the community. Your home may be worth full price  
xxiv Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

to a builder as a result of the lot upon which it sits. If a builder buys the home to rehabilitate or knock down to rebuild, you will not have to incur any expenses to fix it up. In addition, the builder will buy it as is, without any concern for existing home defects—two things that could be a significant problem if you sold it to a buyer seeking to occupy it.  
CHAPTER 1 

**Why Sell By Owner?** 

Savvy homeowners across this country are increasingly choosing to sell their homes by themselves, without real estate agents. In 2001, the National Association of Realtors’ own website, **www\.realtor.org**, estimated that 20% of homeowners sold their home without a broker. Today, that percentage is regarded by many industry watchers to be about 25%. The consensus throughout the industry is that this number will only continue to increase. A few trends have occurred simultaneously to set the stage for this for sale-by-owner phenomenon. 

**We Can Handle New Ideas**  

As we evolve to better accept new ideas, our natural curiosity, in turn, prompts us to further investigate them. Instead of just knowing about the existence of a new subject area, we often choose to explore deeper. The Internet allows us to have more and better information at our fingertips than we had in our entire school’s library. The easy access to new information, coupled with our curiosity, has yielded a do-it-yourself craze. We have become comfortable challenging ourselves to become adept with these  
2 Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

once-unfamiliar areas. The pride achieved and the money saved by doing things yourself are powerful incentives.  

It is this avant-garde attitude and personality that allows us to avail ourselves of the information in this book and elsewhere, and confidently and successfully market and sell our homes without a broker.  

**Extinction of the Middleman** 

The Web changed business forever. One of the Internet’s most drastic impacts stems from the often unguarded access to informa tion it offers. Prior to this, many businesses were successful because of their expert ability to provide specialized information for a fee. Often, a travel agent was consulted so the availability and rates of airline flights and hotel rooms could be compared. Now, in less time than it can take to drive to the local travel agency, a person can log on to his or her computer, compare the rates and availabil ity of several airlines and hotels, see virtual tours of the hotel prop erty, browse the restaurant’s menu, get directions from the airport, and book the entire vacation. The travel agency business has been harshly impacted by the Internet as a result of the ease in which information can be exchanged. 

The real estate agency is predominantly in the same position. It publicizes the availability of a home for sale in hopes of attracting a prospective purchaser. Prior to the Internet, the public would be hard-pressed to learn of the availability, location, and details of a property on the market without contacting a real estate agency. 

The Internet has ended the real estate agents’ monopoly on this information. By simple virtue of its size, the Internet is a much more powerful tool than the Multiple Listing Service system. A cursory search of websites providing real estate information from sellers selling by themselves yields almost 1.5 million results. (A review and evaluation of some of these websites is discussed in Chapter 5.) Within these sites, buyers are able to locate property in any city or town in the nation, learn every needed detail, and  
Why Sell By Owner? 3 

contact the seller directly without any interference from the middleman. Lastly (and not least importantly), the house may be sold without paying an agent’s commission. This brings us to the third trend fueling the for-sale-by-owner growth. 

**A Little (Too Much) Off the Top** 

It is no secret that real estate prices across the nation have risen dra matically over the past few decades. For sellers, it is great news to know that their largest purchase will likely return them a profit when they sell. This is hardly the case with most other purchases, such as automobiles, furniture, office equipment, and even things bought specifically as an investment, like mutual funds. In 1992, the average existing home in the United States sold for \$103,700. In 2004, the average existing home sold for \$191,800, an increase of 85% (or 7% per year). During the same time frame, a typical real estate agency’s fee has remained constant at 5% to 6% of the sales price. In 1992, the agency that sold the average home earned a \$5,703.50 commission, while in 2004 the agency made a \$10,549 commission. This surge in house values has allowed the earnings of real estate agencies during this period to grow at twice the rate of the average worker.  

What has happened as a result of these huge potential profits is what always happens in a market economy. Many outsiders notice the large profits being made in the real estate agency industry, and enter the industry. As a result, many more agencies and agents are now vying for the same business. While the potential number of sales per agent has been reduced because of the increased competi tion, this has not changed the increasingly higher fee that the seller must pay to have an agency sell his or her house. 

At a recent closing I attended, I got into a conversation with one of the real estate agents about how the real estate market was performing. She proudly told me that her office had just listed a luxury home for 1.8 million dollars and that it sold the next day. After inquiry, she admitted that the agency virtually incurred no expenses in the marketing of the home. I then asked whether the  
4 Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

office had volunteered to reduce the approximately \$100,000 com mission. She shook her head, smiled, and stated, *“*Our office does not do that.*”* 

Because broker’s commissions are tied to the sales price, it is very possible that the broker can pocket more money from the sale of the home than the seller. This happened with one of the homes I purchased during the mid-1990s. The seller had purchased the home in the late 1980s, when housing prices were at unprece dented highs. Over the next few years, the market value of the home dropped due to the slow economy. The couple who owned the home were divorcing and decided to sell. As a result of the mortgage and settlement costs, including the broker’s several thousand-dollar commission, the sellers actually had to *pay* money to sell their home to me. Homeowners are beginning to take notice of the fee they will have to pay to the agency, and consequently, are more and more often deciding to attempt to market the home by themselves. 

**Best Candidates for Selling Their Own Homes** As discussed, certain factors have come together to cause the large growth of the number of homeowners who sell their own homes. These factors have changed the world of home selling and apply uni versally to all homeowners. However, while selling your home can be attainable by all, for certain homeowners, it is particularly suit able and highly recommended. Therefore, we next turn to examine those categories of homeowners who, because of their circumstances, absolutely should attempt to sell their homes by themselves. 

**Those Not in a Hurry** 

Everyone who puts his or her house on the market does so with the intent of selling it. No one with this intent wishes to prolong the selling process more than necessary. However, some homeowners, for one reason or another, have the luxury of time.   
Why Sell By Owner? 5 

Some homeowners may want to test the market and agree to sell their home only if they obtain the right price. If they receive this price, then they will find another home; if not, they will take their house off the market.  

Others may have a large window in which to sell their home. For example, homeowners who will be selling their home and moving into a home or condominium community that has yet to be con structed will have at least a few months before they need to sell.  

Similarly, many individuals sell their homes and move into apartments to free up money to enjoy their retirement. They often can move into an apartment without much advance notice, and therefore, can begin the process only when they find a buyer for their home.  

Other homeowners may have a vacation home they may move into after they sell their home, while they search for the ideal new home. Those who sell their investment property and not their res idence may also have the luxury of time.  

Because homeowners in these various types of scenarios have time on their side, they will be better suited toward marketing their homes by themselves. 

**Those Close to Home** 

Selling your home will likely require being available to show it to prospective buyers at various days and times. This will be chal lenging, especially if you work. For this reason, selling your own home is better suited for those who:  

• are retired; 

• work out of the home;  

• work close to home with flexible jobs;  

• have a spouse or other adult at home; or, 

• have a nearby friend or relative who can assist. 

If you do not fit into one of the above-mentioned ideal categories, do not despair. As a by-owner seller, you will be able to schedule  
6 Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

all showings at a time that is convenient for both you and your prospective buyer. This is not always possible when a home is mar keted by an agent. They often only provide a notice to the owner a few minutes before the showing. Many owners who work a distance away from their homes are able to provide showings on evenings and weekends, and this suits many buyers just as well. 

**Those on a Well-Traveled Road** 

*Exposure* is one of the most important keys for selling. For retail businesses, the busier the street it is on, the more customers it can expect. The same is true for homes on well-traveled roads.  

High visibility helps homes on well-traveled roads attract much interest. For the cost of a for sale sign on the front lawn, your home can be advertised to the dozens or hundreds of vehicles that pass by each day. As a result, it may receive more attention than the small and costly ad in the local newspaper. For those with homes in high-visibility areas, your inherent advantage allows you to be well-suited to sell your home by yourself. 

**Those in a Seller’s Market** 

Every so often, a specific geographical region experiences certain conditions that cause it to be a *seller’s market*. These conditions may include one or more of the following:  

• a shortage of homes for sale in the market (commonly described as *low inventory*);  

• low mortgage loan interest rates; 

• a heightened demand for homes; or, 

• rapidly increasing real estate values.  

When one or more of these conditions exist, it is likely a seller’s mar ket. When this occurs, you will often hear of homeowners who are able to sell their homes after only a few days. Often, the homeowner will receive a great deal of interest from prospective buyers and may receive multiple offers. It also is common during a seller’s market for  
Why Sell By Owner? 7 

sellers to receive offers above the asking price. During these periods, the chances of success for a by-owner seller are much greater. 

**Those Selling a Nonunique Property** 

A clothing store sells more pairs of denim jeans than it does alli gator-skin pants. While someone eventually will buy the alligator pants, the jeans greatly outsell them because more of the store’s customers prefer the look and price of the jeans. The same result occurs with the sale of real estate. Uniquely styled homes often take longer to sell than the more traditional home because there are more available buyers for the traditionally styled home.  

Unlike in other countries, people in America buy homes for an intended, finite period. As such, individuals purchase a home knowing that someday they will want to sell it. Therefore, despite an initial inclination toward desiring a unique home—like the house designed like a ship complete with porthole windows—buy ers are mindful of its limited market when it would be their turn to sell. This awareness hinders the demand and makes marketing unique properties more challenging.  

••••• 

The categories discussed in this chapter merely highlight signifi cant home-selling advantages that a seller could exploit to save paying a commission to an agent. While the seller who fits into one or more of the above categories is likely to succeed in selling his or her own home, it does not mean that if you do not fit into any of these categories, you should not try to sell your home your self. If the categories do not apply in your case, you will still be able to apply the concepts and suggestions in this book. Always remember—you will never know if you could have succeeded unless you first try. If you do not have any luck, you can always revert to selling your home with an agent.   
CHAPTER 2 

**Before the For Sale Sign Goes Up**

Once you accept an offer on your home from a buyer, the closing will typically occur within thirty to sixty days. Because the process happens so fast, it is best to be ready for the sale of your home as well as your future after the sale *before* you put the for sale sign in the front lawn. This chapter examines how to strategically plan your sale and move, causing as little disruption in your life as pos sible. The next chapter will explore some of the more active steps that you will need to take to get your home ready to market before the for sale sign goes up. 

**Planning the Sale of Your Home** 

It is recommended that you find a buyer for your home and have it *under agreement* prior to making an offer to buy another. To do oth erwise would place you at risk of carrying both houses, which includes two mortgages, two real estate tax bills, two insurance pre miums, two sets of heating and utility bills––all for an indefinite period of time.   
10 Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

However, even if you wisely place yours on the market first, there is still some significant thinking to be done and questions to be answered.  

• Where are you going once you sell your home?  

• What sort of time will you need to find your new home?  • If you cannot find the right home within that time, do you have a backup plan?  

• Can you rent short-term or move in with relatives?  

• What about the storage of your furniture and possessions?  

These and other related questions should be discussed and answered prior to placing your home on the market. 

Most buyers will take about thirty to sixty days to purchase your home from the date of your acceptance of their offer. *Cash buyers—* those not needing a mortgage loan—may be able to complete the deal even faster. For some, a quick turnaround is not a problem. You may not need to purchase another home upon selling yours, especially if: 

• you will be renting an apartment with a flexible commence ment date;  

• you are selling a rental property or second home; 

• you are moving in with others; or, 

• you have already purchased your new home and were carrying the expenses of two homes simultaneously. 

**Buying a New Home** 

If you fit into one of the previously mentioned categories, ques tions about where you will live are answered, and finding another house in time is irrelevant. However, if you need to buy another home, you have to consider the possible scenarios dis cussed in this chapter.  
Before the For Sale Sign Goes Up  
11 

**Find Another Home in the Required Time** 

Quite likely, you may have to try to locate your new home and pur chase it on or before the day that a buyer buys yours. If you are lucky, your buyer may be willing to increase this time from the normal thirty- to sixty-day period. In any case, you can be sure that having to locate and buy your new residence under such restrictive conditions can lead to much stress.  

**Negotiate a Flexible Closing Date** 

If you do not have a new home to move into, you may sell your home to your buyer only if he or she agrees to a *delayed closing date*, such as ninety days out from your acceptance of the offer (rather than the more typical forty-five days).  

In addition, you may also request that the buyer agree to include a provision in the *Purchase and Sale Agreement* (see Chapter 7), whereby you can move up the closing date upon your finding a new home. This allows you more time to locate the right house so you are not rushed into making this important decision. It also locks in the buyer to buying your home. Further, if you do find the right home right away and no longer need to close so far in the future, you may change the date on which you sell your home to your buyer by providing him or her with the notice that your purchase and sales contract specifies. 

Such flexibility on the buyer’s part is rare, but it does happen. Unsophisticated buyers who are not working with an attorney may agree to this arrangement. A buyer who is currently renting or who is living with family may yield this flexibility to the seller in order to beat out other prospective buyers and make the deal work. These buyers may only need to provide thirty days’ notice to their landlord, or in the case of those living with family, no notice at all. Such flexibility probably will not be available during a buyer’s mar ket, when buyers are few compared to the number of sellers.   
12 Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

**Negotiate a Purchase of a New Home Contingency** One safe way to proceed is to only accept your buyer’s offer for your home *contingent* upon you finding a new home. With this contingency, if you do not find a new home by a specified date, then you need not continue with the sale of your home and the deal will be voided.  

The actual event that needs to occur before you are required to sell your home may vary. It may be based simply upon your offer on another home being accepted, or it may be contingent upon the actual closing on your purchase. In addition, the date by which the specific contingency needs to occur is variable. You can make the contingency only valid within a few days after you accept your buyer’s offer, or the contingency can remain valid through the day before the closing on your sale. The later in the process you request to be able to back out, the more opposition you may expect from your buyer. 

As you might guess, buyers usually are not eager to include such a provision in the sales agreement. It places the risk of you finding a home on them. If you are unsuccessful, their plans are destroyed, whereas you maintain the status quo. Moreover, if your buyer was, in turn, selling his or her home to buy yours, this contingency will likely affect that transaction as well. However, because real estate is so unique, in a buyer’s mind, there may be no satisfactory substi tute for the home he or she seeks to purchase. Buyers who fall head-over-heels for a particular home may be willing to make such a concession to the seller. Additionally, in a seller’s market, the lack of houses on the market may better allow sellers to take advantage of such terms.  

**Rent Back from Your Buyer** 

This option allows you to sell your home to your buyer and still stay in it until you are able to move. It is somewhat commonly employed by sellers who are moving into a new house or housing complex that is under construction, and an exact move-in date is  
Before the For Sale Sign Goes Up  
13 

not certain. It works best with buyers who do not have to sell a house in order to buy and who are flexible with their move-in date.  Although the buyer may be flexible about when he or she moves in, the mortgage restrictions will typically require him or her to schedule the purchase before the interest rate his or her lender committed to on the loan expires (the *rate-lock expiration date*). Consequently, the buyer can satisfy the lender’s restriction and still be flexible for you by agreeing to buy the home, and have you continue to occupy it while paying a periodic *use and occu pancy* fee until the agreed-upon move-out date. The standard mort gage requires the buyer to physically move into the home within sixty days of the closing, so most buyers will not agree to have you stay beyond this period. 

As with the *purchase of a new home* contingency, most buyers will not be overly eager to grant you this courtesy. Having you live in their home while they pay the mortgage and hope that you leave when you promise understandably carries significant risk. However, buyers who desire your property will often be willing to accommodate you.  

The *Indemnification Agreement to Remain in the Property* that would be executed identifies the parties’ respective rights and obli gations, and eliminates most of the buyer’s risk. This agreement will seek to resolve such issues as:  

• what rate the seller will pay for use and occupancy;  

• how long the seller may continue to reside in the home after the closing; 

• who will be responsible for the utilities, taxes, and insurance during the period;  

• whether the seller will pay a security deposit to protect the buyer if damages occur during the seller’s occupancy; and, • what the penalty will be if seller fails to move out when promised.

**Move into Temporary Housing** 

If your buyer does not agree to one of the options listed above, and you are not able to locate a satisfactory home by the date for your sale, your only option will be to find temporary housing.  

Home sellers in this position commonly put their possessions in storage and move into an apartment, into an extended-stay hotel, or in with relatives on a short-term basis while they continue their search for a new home. This option works well for sellers who are building a new home or moving into a new condominium complex still under construction. In these cases, their exact move-in date is likely undeterminable, and this option

**Marketplace**

Preparing a home cosmetically for sale is common sense, but it needs to be mentioned. I often hear from clients who view proper ties and are immediately turned off as a result of certain conditions the seller could have rectified quickly and inexpensively. You can not please everyone with the amenities and features your home has, but you should strive to take care of the little things. Buyers are looking for properties that are neat and have been cared for properly. 

**Start Outside** 

You never get a second chance to make a good first impression. You have probably heard this before, but it applies here as well. The first thing buyers notice when they come to view your property is the landscaping.  

**Landscaping** 

A nicely landscaped lawn can increase the value of your home, often allowing the homeowner to recover all of a landscaping investment. Depending on the costs incurred and the amount the   
16 Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

home’s sale price increased, you could actually recover more than what was spent on landscaping.  

Psychologically, when buyers see well-trimmed landscaping, they believe that the owner takes pride in the home, and therefore, the home has been well cared for and not abused. Consequently, they believe that there has been less wear and tear, and that there will be less maintenance needed down the road for the new owners.  

**House Exterior** 

After the landscaping, the prospective buyer next sees the exterior of the home. Nothing does more for the exterior than a fresh, new coat of paint. Although it can cost thousands of dollars, a new coat will add vibrancy. If a new coat is not needed or money is tight, consider touching up some of the faded areas and areas of greatest exposure to your prospective buyer, such as the front door and trim, as well as other entrance areas. If you have an exterior that does not require paint, such as vinyl siding, consider giving it a wash and scrub using the recommended surface-specific solution. 

**Move Inside** 

Walls have a tendency to show the most wear and tear inside a home. Because walls are by definition vertical and in direct eye sight of buyers viewing the home, your prospective buyer will readily notice imperfections such as children’s (and adults’) handprints, scuffmarks, divots, nail holes, and stickers in the children’s areas. Just as well-kept landscaping causes the buyer to presume positive attributes about the rest of the home, banged-up walls will cause the buyer to presume the home has suffered from a lack of atten tion, and that defects could materialize after his or her purchase.  

**Painting the Interior** 

Painting is an especially wise investment as you prepare to sell your home, because it is a task a non-handy person can do well without too much effort. Despite the current popularity, resist the temptation  
Getting Your Home Ready for the Marketplace 17 

to choose a loud and vibrant color for your paint. Soft off-whites and light, neutral colors will make your rooms appear larger, and will likely match with your prospective buyer’s furniture. 

**Professional Carpet Cleaning** 

Beyond painting, there are other small projects that will help you efficiently achieve the neat and clean look that is valued by buyers. Professionally clean all carpeting. Stains in carpets only remind a prospective buyer than this is a *used* house. Moreover, the buyer may be forced to assume that the stains will not come out and that new carpeting is needed, thereby diminishing the value of the home in his or her eyes. Professional carpet cleaning should remove most stains, and will leave the room with a fresh and clean aroma.  

**Professional House Cleaner** 

In the bathroom and kitchen, re-grout the tile and backsplash so that all crevices are pure white. Replace aged shower curtains and scrub the tub, or if necessary, have a new tub surface professionally installed. If you have a fireplace, clean it thoroughly and remove all soot. For under \$100 for most homes, a professional house cleaner can come in and clean all the rooms and surfaces. Afterward, if you found the right person, the house will sparkle and smell wonderful.  

**Remodeling** 

Larger remodeling projects, done merely for the purpose of increasing the value of the home for a sale, are (for the most part) impractical. Ideally, you should undertake a remodeling project only if you can expect to stay in the house for a while and enjoy it before deciding to sell. However, some remodeling may be in order after careful consideration.  

**Best Investment** 

In a recent annual “Cost vs. Value Report,” *Remodeling Magazine* found that minor kitchen remodeling in the \$15,000–cost category  
18 Sell Your Home Without a Broker 

gave the best return on investment. For a kitchen project of this size, home owners could expect to recoup 92.0% of their investment at the time of sale. After this, in descending order came the replacement of siding (92.8% return); the mid-range remodeling of a bathroom (90.1% return); the addition of a deck (86.7% return); and, the addi tion of a mid-range bathroom (86.4% return). Interestingly, the addi tion of a sunroom was determined to have the lowest return on investment, at just under a 71% return. 

**Make the Worst Room the Best** 

When deciding on which remodeling project to undertake, in addition to considering the report results previously mentioned, consider turning the worst part of your home into the best. In many homes, there are one or two particular rooms that lag signif icantly behind the others. For example, in one home, the kitchen may have been neglected for thirty years and is in desperate need of updating, while in another home, the kitchen and baths may be reasonably well-appointed, but the living room is dark and gloomy with matted carpeting. In each instance, if these respective rooms are overhauled, the overall appearance of the home is increased greater than if any other room were to be overhauled. 

**Working with Tradespeople** 

While remodeling should be enjoyed by the owner and not under taken merely to help a sale, there is another reason why such projects should not be done on the eve of putting your home on the market. Unfortunately, it is common for disputes to occur between the trades person and the homeowner. Often, the tradesman’s progress is not at the pace expected by the owner, causing the owner to terminate the contract in the middle of the job. Other times, as a result of *unfore seen obstacles*, the tradesperson’s final bill is higher than the estimate. In other cases, the homeowner is not satisfied about the tradesper son’s finished product and holds back payment. Also, there is the case where the homeowner’s taste is larger than his or her wallet, and  
Getting Your Home Ready for the Marketplace 19 

money runs out before the tradesperson has completed the work. In any of these scenarios, a dispute will arise between the parties.  The law will allow the unpaid tradesman to file a *mechanic’s lien* on the owner’s home. The lien will be recorded at the applicable registry of deeds and will cause there to be an *encumbrance* on the owner’s title, much like a mortgage. The typical mechanic’s lien statute allows a tradesperson to *perfect a lien* on the property for work done to the home within the last ninety days. Therefore, a well-timed mechanic’s lien filing by your tradesperson could jeopardize your sale, delay it, or cause you to have the value claimed due by the tradesperson held back from the sale proceeds until the matter is resolved. This could be devastating if you were relying on the full proceeds of the sale to purchase your new home later that day.

This is often true when you have lived in your home for several years. Things accumulate and make a home feel and look small and cluttered. This is certainly not a positive char acteristic in the eyes of buyers. When buyers see lots of stuff stored in the basement, in the attic, in the closets, in the garage, and on the front and back porches, they are bound to consciously or sub consciously think at least one of the following.

• *If they do try to move all of this stuff out, will they scratch or dam age the walls and floors in the process?*

**Working with an Attorney** 

Having an attorney represent you when you buy or sell real estate is always a wise decision. When you sell a home without a real estate broker, an attorney is of even greater value. For sellers not using a broker, an attorney will have somewhat of a dual role, and you should approach him or her for broker-oriented matters, such as marketing suggestions and advice to better evaluate the offers. 

Even though you do not have your home on the market yet, now is the time for you to find and locate an attorney. The longer in the process you wait to find an attorney to advise you, the
